RECORDS
WEDNESDAY, APRIL 29, 1914
The Annual Convention of Psi Upsilon was called to order at 8:15
P. M. at the Narragansett Hotel, Providence, R. I., by Brother George
S. Coleman, a delegate of the Executive Council. Bro. Coleman ap
pointed Bro. James G. Affleck, Jr. (Sigma '14) Temporary President
and Bro. Maurice A. Wolf (Sigma '14) Temporary Recorder. Bro.
Affleck took the chair and appointed the following committees:
Committee on Credentials�
Bros. Chester A. Minds (Tau '14),
Chairman; William S. Jenkins, Jr. (Iota '14) and Robert B. Corcoran
(Omega '16)
Committee on Permanent Organization�
^Bros. Robert S. Hold
ing, Jr. (Sigma '14), Chairman; Stephen B. Story (Theta '14) and
John C. Evans (Rho '14)
The meeting then adjourned until Thursday, 10 a. m., at the same
place.

Bro. Waugh (delegate of the Council) submitted the following
resolution :
Resolved, That the matter of the Psi Upsilon publication be con
tinued as unfinished business before the Executive Council, and that that
body be and is authorized to establish such publication if and when the
Alumni address rolls are
sufficiently complete.
Under the rules the resolution was referred to the Committee on
Unfinished Business.
[The Convention then went into Committee of the Whole with VicePresident Sawyer in the chair and heard the representatives from the
Pi Upsilon Society of the University of Kansas, Messrs. Carson and
Burket. The regular session was then resumed.]

Appendix A

7
The following matters were referred to the several committees:
To the Committee on New Business the petitions of Phi Kappa Society
of the University of Washington, of Pi Upsilon Society of the University
of Kansas and of Chi Delta Psi Society of the University of Toronto,
bronze tablets of Founders and Chapter insignia; to the Committee on
Unfinished Business the Fraternity publication. Chapter address lists
and expenses of delegates to Convention; to the Committee to Nominate
Members of the Executive Council the nomination of members to fill
the vacancies caused by the expiration of the terms of Brothers Bridg
man and Coleman; to the Committee on Annual Communication the
Treasurer's report and Chapter visitations.
The meeting then adjourned until Friday morning. May 1, 10 A. M.,
at the same
place.
FRIDAY, MAY 1
Meeting called to order at 10:30 A. m.. President Coleman in the
chair.
Minutes of previous day were read and approved.
The Committee on Credentials reported that Bro. Paul Churchill
De Wolf (Sigma '05) had been elected graduate delegate. The report
was accepted.
Bro. McLaren (Epsilon) reported for the Committee to Nominate
Members of the Executive Council the nomination of Bros. Herbert
Lawrence Bridgman (Oamma '66) and George Silas Coleman (Xi '76)
to succeed themselves for the term ending 1919. Bros. Bridgman and
Coleman were thereupon duly elected. Bro. Coleman expressed on be
half of his colleague and himself sincere appreciation of the honor con
ferred upon them.
Bro. Stevens (Chi) reported for the Committee on Unfinished Busi
ness the following resolutions:
I. Referring back to the Coimcil the matter of a Psi Upsilon
publication. Unanimously adopted (General Resolution No. 1) .
II. Referring back to the Council the compilation and publication
of Chapter address lists and submitting to the Council the matter of a
new general Catalogue. Unanimously adopted ( General Resolution No. 2 ) .

9
VIII. Providing for bronze tablets of the Foimdera for the Omicron
and Delta Delta Chapters and for possible future use.
Unanimously
adopted. (General Resolution No. 13)
Bro. Young (Delta) offered a resolution that the Convention put
itself on record as
being opposed to any scheme of District Conventions
in Psi Upsilon, the resolution not to apply to District Conferences. On
roll-call the vote was as follows:
Yeas�
Delta, Upsilon, Phi, Eta, Tau, Omega, Omicron.
Nays�
Theta, Sigma, Beta, Oamma, Zeta, Lambda, Kappa, Psi,
Xi, Iota, Pi, Chi, Mu, Rho, Epsilon, Delta Delta.
Bro. Brooks (Upsilon) offered a resolution that the matter of
delegates' expenses to conventions be referred back to the Executive
Council. Unanimously adopted. (General Resolution No. 14)
Bro. Affleck (Sigma) offered a resolution providing that the Con
vention of 1915 be held with the Epsilon Chapter. Unanimously adopted.
(General Resolution No. 15)
[The Convention then went into Committee of the Whole to hear
the representatives of Chi Delta Psi Society of Toronto University,
Vice-President Henshaw (Sigma) in the chair. After the hearing Presi
dent Coleman resumed the chair.]
The Chair announced that the Committee on Entertainment had
been waiting half an hour for the Convention to adjourn in order to
carry out the program for the day. On motion Bros. Stevens (Chi) and
Kennedy (Mu) were appointed a Special Committee to prepare a resolu
tion in memoriam the late Bro. William Whitman Bailey (Sigma '64)
and a resolution of thanks and congratulations to the Sigma Chapter
for its generous hospitality; the resolutions to be submitted to the
Recorder and printed in the Records of the Convention.*
The Chair thanked the delegates for their prolonged and careful at
tention to business, and at 2:10 p. m. declared the Convention adjourned
sine die.
RespectfuUy submitted
Maurice Augustus Wolf
(Sigma '14)
Recorder

General Resolution No. 10�
Resolved, That in view of the fact that
several of the Chapters of the Fraternity have not received sufficient
information concerning Phi Kappa Society and the situation at the
University of Washington, the petition of Phi Kappa should be sub
mitted again to the individual Chapters of the Fraternity for their
consideration.
General Resolution No. 11�
Whereas, This Fraternity is not and
never will be too large for direct and informal relations between the
Council and Chapters, supplemented by relations between the Chapters;
and
Whereas, the Fraternity has heretofore disapproved of a
Traveling
Secretary because of the expense and the consequent necessity of increas
ing the individual tax.
Be it Resolved, That this Convention go on record as opposed to a
Traveling Secretary; and
Be it further Resolved, That each Chapter of the Fraternity should
be visited by a member of the Council at least once in every three years.
General Resolution No. 12�
Resolved, That inasmuch as the Epsilon,
Omicron and Delta Delta Chapters have been admitted to the Fraternity
since the official adoption of Chapter Insignia prepared by the late
Brother Albert Poole Jacobs (Phi '73) for the other Chapters, the
Executive Council be and hereby is authorized to secure
insignia for the
Epsilon, Omicron and Delta Delta Chapters in conformity with the sys
tem heretofore adopted.
General Resolution No. 13�
Resolved, That the Executive Council
procure for the Omicron and Delta Delta Chapters bronze tablets of the
Founders similar to the tablet designed by Brother William Ordway
Partridge (Lambda '85) in 1907, and several additional tablets for possi
ble future use.
General Resolution No. 14�
Resolved, That the matter of apportion
ing the expenses of one
delegate from each Chapter to the Annual Con
vention be referred back to the Executive Council for report at the next
Convention.
General Resolution No. 15�
Resolved, That the Convention of 1915
be held with the Epsilon Chapter at some time between August 15 and
September 15 of that year.

12
special eesolutions
Special Resolution No. 1�
Resolved, That the Convention sincerely
regrets the inability of Brother WiUiam Howard Taft (Beta '78) to be
present.*
Special Resolution No. 2�
Resolved, That the hearty thanks and
congratulations of the Convention be tendered to the Sigma Chapter for
its generous hospitality, its varied and interesting program of events and
the delightful manner in which every feature of its entertainment was
successfully presented.
Special Resolution No. 3�
Resolved, That this Convention record its
profound sorrow at the recent death of Brother William Whitman Bailey,
Sigma '64, whose long, honorable and useful career as scholar, teacher,
author, poet and citizen endeared him to thousands of his countrymen,
and whose constant love for Psi Upsilon and devotion to her interests
entitle him to the lasting and grateful remembrance of the Fraternity.
*
Though prevented from atteudlns the Convention, Brother Taft sent a characteristic
message over the long distance telephone from New Haven to Brother Norman S Dike
(Sigma '85), who was Toastmaster at the Banquet, and Brother Dike repeated the
message to the banqueters.

CONVENTION OF 1914
Membership. The Active membership of the Fraternity reported
as of February 1st, 1914, was 658, as against 613 for 1913. The Council
desires to commend the very marked improvement in the form of the
Annual Reports submitted by the Chapters this year.

This long list contains the names of many brethren who had be
come distinguished in various walks of life, and of many who, if not
widely known, had yet endeared themselves to others by useful and
honorable service. In the death of Brother Goodale, Theta '38, in his
ninety-eighth year, the Fraternity lost its oldest member. The badge
placed on his breast by the Founders was worn by him until the end,
and now through the kindness of his nieces and at the suggestion of
Brother William K. Wickes, Gamma '70, it has become the property of
the Fraternity, and in suitable frame will be preserved and cherished.
To those who had the good fortune to know Brother William Whit
man Bailey, of the Sigma, and particularly to the members of his own
Chapter, under whose auspices we meet to-day, his recent death so
shortly before Convention was indeed pathetic.
Chapter Letters. The Council has noted with pleasure, during
the year, the improved tone of Chapter Letters, possibly due to the
earnest suggestions of delegates to the last Convention. Without sacri
ficing the humorous, social or friendly spirit, the correspondents have
managed to discuss matters of common interest. The letters may be
come a convenient means of exchanging views in advance of possible
action by Convention. Two subjects frequently mentioned during the
year were Traveling Secretary and Territorial Conventions, each of
sufficient importance to justify thorough consideration before final action.
Chapter Address Lists. The Convention of 1913 provided that at
the expense of the General Fund the Council should publish a first edi-

The inference apparently to be drawn from this data is that the
average appropriation for a delegate to a Convention held east of
Buffalo will be about $50. However, no reUable estimate can be made
for Conventions held in other places.
Unless the Convention is now
prepared to indicate a definite policy
as to the apportionment of delegates' expenses, and payment thereof
from the General Fund, the Council recommends that the matter be
carefully considered by the Chapters and final action deferred until the
next Convention.
Phi KIappa Society. The adverse vote of the Tau Chapter (re
cently reported to the Council) on the application of the Phi Kappa
Society of the University of Washington for a charter of the Fraternity
prevents the establshment of a chapter at said University upon the
petition presented last year. Several of the Chapters had voted favora
bly on the petition; several had expressed favorable opinions; several
had expressed adverse inclinations; and others had expressed uncer
tainty and a desire to hear more on the subject at the present Conven
tion. The Council has been advised that a new
petition will be pre
sented this year,* and submits herewith a letter from the Psi Upsilon
Alumni Association of Pudget Sound, Washington, signed by Brother
A. P. Sawyer, Beta '80, President, and by forty other members of the
Association.t
Chapter Visitations. Pursuant to the provisions of the Consti
tution, and to the requests of the Chapters, the Council has endeavored,
during the past year, to arrange for systematic visitations by its mem
bers of the various institutions where our chapters are located, with a
view to securing such information concerning the personnel, activities
and standing of the members, and the standing and influence of the
Chapters, and such information concerning the institutions themselves,
as may be comprehensive and useful. The member of the Council mak
ing a visit is expected to report in writing to the Council, and to pre
pare a copy of his report for transmission to the Chapter visited. Since
the last Convention, official visits have been made to the Sigma, Upsilon,
Iota, Phi, Mu, Rho, Omega and Omicron; an official visit will be made
to the Kappa on April 29th, and to the Delta early in May; and unoffi
cial visits have been made to the Theta, Delta, Beta, Oamma, Ohi and

Eta. Official visits to Beta Beta and Delta Delta are planned for
May. To the members of the Council at least the Chapter visits have
been full of interest, and it is believed that without undue expense every
Chapter of the Fraternity could be formally visited by a member of the
Council at least once in every three years.
Pi Upsilon of Kansas. A new petition from the Pi Upsilon Fra
ternity of the University of Kansas has been presented and is herewith
submitted,* together with a letter from the Missouri Valley Alumni
Association of Psi Upsilon, signed by Brother James H. Austin, Theta
'67, President, Eldon C. Hemenway, Psi '07, Secretary, and by twentythree other members.f We are advised that representatives of the So
ciety will be in Providence at the time of the Convention, and would ap
preciate the courtesy of a hearing.
Chi Delta Psi. The Chi Delta Psi Society of the University of
Toronto will this year renew its petition for a charter,} and begs the
privilege of a hearing.
Eightieth Anniversary. The Eightieth Anniversary of the Found
ing of the Fraternity was
duly celebrated on November 24, 1913 in New
York City under the joint auspices of the Fraternity and the Psi Up
silon Club. Four hundred and fifty members of the Fraternity gathered
at the Waldorf-Astoria for the occasion. Brother Herbert L. Bridgman,
Oamma '66, presided; Brother William M. Kingsley, Delta '83, was
Toastmaster, and the Speakers were: Brothers William Howard Taft,
Beta '78, John C. Spooner, Rho '64, William K. Wickes, Oamma '70,
Bishop James H. Darlington, Delta '77, and Alfred E. Stearns, Gamma '94.
The Dinner courses were interspersed with lantern slides of the
Founders and other prominent Alumni, of the Chapter houses, of Con
vention Groups, of the Badge, Insignia, and Flag, and of Brothers
William Whitman Bailey, Sigma '64, and Charles Mills Gayley, Phi '78,
with stanzas of the songs written by them expressly for the Anniversary
(Sing the Glad Praises and The Pilgrims), which have been copyrighted
and adopted as Fraternity Songs.
The Eightieth Anniversary was duly celebrated also by the Psi
Upsilon Clubs and Associations of Chicago, Detroit and San Francisco.

The Psi Upsilon Club of Chicago has taken a new lease of life. It
has Headquarters at the Hotel La Salle, has increased its membership,
and promises to be an active influence for the good of the Fraternity.
Bronze Tablets of Founders. Arrangements have been made for
procuring six additional bronze tablets commemorative of the Founders,
similar to those designed by Brother William Ordway Partridge,
Lambda '85, in 1907, and now installed in all the Chapters except
Omicron and Delta Delta. It is proposed to furnish tablets to the
Omicron and Delta Delta, and to retain four tablets for possible future
use.
Chapter Insignia. The Council suggests that as the Epsilon
Omicron and Delta Delta Chapters have been admitted to the Fraternity
since the official adoption of heraldic insignia prepared by the late
Brother Albert Poole Jacobs, Phi '73, for the other Chapters, insignia
in conformity with the system heretofore adopted should be prepared
for the Epsilon, Omicron and Delta Delta Chapters, and that the Council
be authorized to secure such insignia for those Chapters.
Business Information. The report of the Committee on Business
Information, received from Brother Earl D. Babst, Phi '93, its chairman,
is submitted herewith as part of this communication.*
The Council. The officers of the Council for the past year have
been the same as for the previous year, except that Brother Wertheimer
(Iota '99) has been Recorder in place of Brother Whiting (Tau '88).
Ten meetings have been held and copies of the minutes forwarded to the
Chapters and to various Alumni Associations.
The terms of Brother Bridgman (Oamma '66) and Brother Cole
man (Xi '76) expire with this Convention, and two members are to be
elected for the terms ending in 1919.
Treasurer's Report. The report of the Treasurer is submitted
herewith.t

By Herbert L. Bridgman, President

February 28th, 1914.
To the President
AND Executive Council and Chapters of Psi Upsilon.
Dear Brothers: �
The members of the Puget Sound, Washington, Psi Upsilon Alumni
Association, are
deeply interested in the application for a chapter of Psi
Upsilon at the University of Washington, which was referred by the last
Convention to the various chapters for action.
We do not think it necessary or desirable, at this time, to make
detailed arguments supporting this application as such arguments already
have been presented to the Convention.
We wish, however, to call attention to certain salient facts. The
members of our Association, over fifty in number, three-fourths of whom
reside in Seattle, where the University of Washington is located, are all
agreed, after a
study of the question and careful personal investigation,
extending over a
period of upwards of four years, that the University of
Washington is now of Psi Upsilon rank, compares favorably with other
large universities in this country and is in every way worthy of a chapter
of our fraternity.
We also are agreed that the Phi Kappa fraternity, which is petition
ing for a charter, is composed of men carefully selected from more than
two thousand male students. This conclusion has not been reached
hastily. Not only have the members of Phi Kappa met the tests imposed
by the older Psi Upsilon Alumni, but, they have met the more severe
tests which are necessary to satisfy those of the Alumni who have grad
uated within recent years, and upon whom college and fraternity traditions
still have a strong hold. In view of these facts, we feel that we have at
hand the material for the making of a
strong chapter of Psi Upsilon.
Another point that we ask you to consider is the position of the
Epsilon chapter. Epsilon is practically isolated, located more than two
thousand miles from the nearest chapter of the fraternity.
"
The members
of Epsilon, naturally and rightly, desire another chapter of Psi Upsilon

26
on the Pacific Coast. To that end it has made a careful study of condi
tions at the University of Washington and of the fitness of Phi Kappa
to be admitted to Psi Upsilon. These investigations have been carried on
over a
period of three years, both by Alumni and undergraduates, and have
resulted in an unanimous vote by Epsilon for the admission of Phi Kappa
to Psi Upsilon.
As good "Psi U's" all of us believe in our own
chapter and of the
particular crowd of which we were members in our
undergraduate days.
This set a high standard for those whom we selected as our successors in
our own chapter and it is not a sentiment that has grown less strong with
the passage of time. We believe Phi Kappa measures up to our standards,
and that the good name of Psi Upsilon, and her interests will not suffer if
committeed to Phi Kappa's keeping.
There is another side of this question, which we acknowledge should
not have preponderating infiuence in the face of adverse conditions, but
should be given due consideration, when conditions are favorable, as in
this case, that is, the desire of the Psi Upsilon Alumni here to have a
chapter of our
fraternity closer at hand, to serve as a
rallying point for
the brothers and to serve as a
stronger bond to draw them closer to each
other and to the fraternity at large.
As we have said before we have the names of more than fifty Alumni
on our rolls. We keep up an active organization, although we are over
nine hundred miles distant from the nearest chapter and twice that dis
tant from the next nearest. Throughout the long years that have
separated some of us from our active fraternity days, we have been loyal
to Psi Upsilon and its traditions, can not you see your way clear, to rely
upon our
judgment, coming as we do from
colleges and universities
throughout the land represnting more than two-thirds of the chapters of
our fraternity, and reward the loyalty we have given to Psi Upsilon, by
giving to the men, whom we have with great care
selected, a charter to
the fraternity that means so much to us?
If you will do this, as brothers, we give you our
pledge, that the
chapter of Psi Upsilon, if established, at the
University of Washington,
will meet every test that Psi UpsUon imposes and will be the leading
fraternity at that University.
Yours in the bonds
A. P. Sawyer, Beta '80
Pres. Puget Sound Alumni Ass'n.

To the Members of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity,
In Convention Assembled, Greetings :
We, the Alumni members of Psi Upsilon, who are located in and near
Kansas City hereby endorse without reservation the petition of the Pi
Upsilon Society for the granting to them of a chapter of Psi Upsilon at
the University of Kansas. After careful investigation we can
urge your
favorable consideration of their request.
We have been influenced to lend our unqualified approval and en
dorsement of this petition and petitioning body through a number of
salient facts.
First. We desire that an active chapter of our fraternity be located
in this vicinity, whereby old associations can be renewed and strengthened.
Second. The University of Kansas is fully worthy of consideration as
a location for a
chapter aa it is one of the most important of the State
Universities and is growing yearlj'. The enrollment is close to three
thousand. It holds sixth place in the number of Liberal Arts students
in this country, and is strong in its separate schools of Science, Engi
neering, Law and Medicine. The University of Kansas is purely an
academic and professional institution, the agricultural and normal col
leges being located elsewhere in the state.
Third. The University of Kansas is located forty miles from Kansis City, which city has a population of over three hundred fifty thousand
and is rapidly growing in importance, as evidenced by the establishment

30
of a Federal Reserve Bank there. An important factor in favor of the
granting of a chapter at Ann Arbor was its proximity to Detroit, which
has always furnished strong men for our fraternity, and Kansas City
would do the same thing for a chapter at Lawrence.
Fourth: There are five alumini of Psi Upsilon as members of the
University of Kansas faculty, headed by the Chancellor of the institution.
Dr. Frank Strong, all of whom enthusiastically endorse the local society.
This organization was founded more than five years ago, has maintained
its own house during all that time and has successfully competed with
all fraternities at the University. It is strongly represented in all
branches of student activities.
Fifth: It is our belief that sooner or later Psi Upsilon must estab
lish a chapter at this important State University, and it appeals to us
that the time is now
ripe for such a move. To install a chapter now
would strongly intrench us in this important territory and give us first
call upon the best men of the institution. Recognition of the local organ
ization of Pi Upsilon, already firmly established, will be a benefit to our
fraternity in the course of its becoming a
truly national organization.
